Press Conferences ¶ 8393 

Text of October 8, 1971 press conference of Secretary of Treasury John B. 

Connally.

SECRETARY CONNALLY: Good afternoon. Thank you all for being here. If I may, I will take a few minutes to briefly outline the details of the 

President's speech last night, and the actions he has taken with respect to the Stabilization Program that will begin on November 14, at the expiration of the Wage/Price Freeze.

As many of you know, the President is committed in his fight against inflation in this Country. He is determined to continue that fight to bring down the rate of inflation; and a goal of 2% to 3% on the rate of inflation has been established as a goal to be achieved by the end of 1972. 

Now, with that in mind, he has created several Boards and Commissions: 

First, the Pay Board:

The Pay Board will be composed of 15 people-five from Labor; five from Business; and five Public Members, one of whom will serve as Chairman. All fifteen will be appointed by the President. 

They will have the jurisdiction, the authority, and the responsibility for setting the standards and criteria relating to pay in this Country: Wages, Salary, Fringe Benefits. They will make the decisions. 

They will grant the exemptions, if any.

They will determine what action is necessary to cure and alleviate inequities that, unquestionably existed—and do exist-during the Freeze period. 

He has also created a Price Commission, which is composed of seven public members. The Chairman will be a full time Member, as will the 

Chairman of the Pay Board. 

The Chairman of the Price Commission will also be named by the 

President, as will all of the Members.

The Price Commission will have jurisdiction over prices in this Country. 

They will have jurisdiction over rents.

They will have jurisdiction over windfall profits and, in addition, they will set their own standards and criteria by which they will, also, attempt to achieve the goals which the President has set in his fight against inflation. 

They will make the decisions, case by case. 

They will grant the exemptions.

They will permit the increases as their own standards and criteria justify. 

Their decisions will be final, as will the decisions of the Pay Board. They are not to be appealed to the Cost of Living Council. 

In addition, the President has created a Committee on Interest and Dividends, which will be chaired by Dr. Arthur Burns, Chairman of the 

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. All of the Members that will serve on that particular Committee will also be Public Members; all 

Government Members.

These are the essential actions which he took. 

There are one or two other matters that I think are important, also, to point out:

¶ 8393

He has enlarged the Productivity Commission, to bring to it the representatives of the Consumer interests and Agricultural interests. It already contains representatives of Labor and Management throughout the Country, but the Productivity Commission will, in the future, be used, in addition to its regular work and studies that are now under way, as an Advisory group to the Cost of Living Council. 

In addition, a Health Services Industry Committee, Advisory Committee, will be created for the purpose of advising both the Pay Board, and the Price Commission, as well as the Cost of Living Council, on policies and actions that are deemed advisable to that particular field. 

There will also be an Advisory group on State and Local Government Actions, particularly in the wage field. They will serve as an Advisory group to the Pay Board as well as the Cost of Living Council. 

I think I should make clear to you at the outset, and stress at the outset, that the Freeze will continue through November 13 of this year. Beginning on the next day, November 14, the Freeze will still be in effect-subject to whatever standards and criteria the two principal Boards set, in the meantime. That is to say, the Pay Board has now 37 days, as does the Price 

Commission-it has 37 days in which to establish standards and criteria by which they intend to operate, and under which they intend to operate, in the period following the expiration of the Freeze on November 13. 

Now, this is a relatively short period of time in one sense, and a relatively long period in another. I think it is ample, in any event, for them to get on board; to establish their own operating procedures; and to begin to make the decisions that must be made, so that there will be no hiatus; and so that the people in this Country can understand what they will be confronted with on November 14 in the Stabilization Program that will follow the Freeze.

I again want to point out that, with respect to the 15 Members of the Pay Board and the 7 Members of the Price Commission, that they each should understand that it is going to be their responsibility, and they will have the authority, to set their own standards; their own criteria for balancing the equities; alleviating inequities; alleviating hardships; granting exceptions, or exemptions. That will be their decision. And they should understand that from the very outset, because the Cost of Living Council does not anticipate, nor want, nor expect, nor will we accept them passing the buck up to the Cost of Living Council. Their decisions in the Pay field, and in the Price field, are going to be final. They will not be appealed to the Cost of Living Council. 

With those general comments, I think, to give you a broad brush picture of the type of mechanisms that are being established, that will be operating in the days ahead, I will attempt now to take any questions. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, as you probably know, 

Organized Labor has withheld its formal announcement of support of this plan because of misgivings about the authority and jurisdiction of the Pay Board. Some of that, I think you may have cleared up, but the question remains, as a result of the briefings in the White House last night: Will the 

Cost of Living Council have any authority to review, to modify, or possibly to veto the standards set by the Pay Board? 

SECRETARY CONNALLY: The Cost of Living Council is not going to veto actions of the Pay Board, or the Price Commission. Now, the Cost of 

Living Council is an arm of the President and it will, for the President, continue to function as it is now constituted. It will have an overall responsibility in the field, for the President. ¶ 8393

It will have an overall review of the actions of the Pay Board, and the Price Commission, and the Commission on Interest and Dividends, first, to be sure there is balance between these separate entities; 

Secondly, to be sure, for the President, in order that we might be able to advise the President about the progress that is being made in achieving his goal now.

I think it is fair to say that, although we certainly don't intend to have to approve the standards and criteria adopted by either of these Boards, nor do we intend to veto their actions on specific case decisions, or their standards of criteria, I think it is fair to say that the Government is going to continue to be in this picture and, if it does become apparent that the actions that are being taken by any of these Boards-whether it is the Interest and Dividend Commission; whether it is the Price Commission; or whether it is the Pay 

Board-if they are not in consonance with the President's announced goal of holding inflation down, then, frankly, some action will have to be taken. 

All I want to make clear is that the Government is not getting out of this picture. 

Now, we are saying that we have tried to structure a mechanism here that will involve the participation of all elements of this Society. The President made very clear last night that he thought that the success of the Freeze had been extraordinary. He thought it had been wonderful-the reaction of the American people, and their participation, and their cooperation. 

He made it clear-and I want to again make it clear today-that the success of this Stabilization Program that will follow on the Freeze, is going to be dependent to a very large extent upon the voluntary compliance by the American people.

Now, with that assumption-that very basic assumption-we have tried to structure it in such a way that all elements of the economy will participate in the decisions that are going to be made. This is why you have a tri-partite 

Pay Board: Five Labor people; five Management people; five Public people.

We understood, very frankly, after many consultations that many of us had the President himself met a little over 600 individuals, representing over 300 organizations-it became clear that at least it was our understanding that this was the type of structure that Labor felt they could work with, that they could cooperate with.

We need their help. We want their help, obviously: Labor organized, and unorganized-particularly Union Labor-is a very strong force in this American economy, and we would hope that they would cooperate. We would hope that they will serve on this Commission, because, without them it is going to be extremely difficult. There is no point in that. We all have the same objective. They want to hold down the cost-of-living increases. They want to stop the rate of inflation.

The working people-Union and non-Union-throughout this Country, made it abundantly clear over the past several weeks that they are in support of the President's program. We have tried to structure a system here that will work fairly and equitably, and permit various elements to participatenot just participate, but make the decisions under which they are going to have to live. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, let me follow that up. If

Organized Labor should convince the Pay Board to allow the increases that are already written in existing contracts to go into effect after the Freeze- 

¶ 8393

and that is one of Labor's very strong positions-would the Administration guarantee George Meany now that the Cost of Living Council would not step in and say, "But that violates the general guidelines"?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: We are not going to guarantee anything to any individual but we certainly have said—and I want to repeat againthat the decision as to whether or not the deferred increases in wage negotiations, and wage contracts is allowed-is a matter for the Pay Board to determine.

Now, they have to determine it in the light of the responsibility that they have, and the goal which they seek. The goal that they have to seek, is the President's goal of a rate of inflation not to exceed two to three percent by the end of 1972.

If they grant the deferred increases, some of them are quite high. This simply means, as they go along in the weeks and months ahead, probably they will have less leeway in other matters, but that is something for them to decide. We are not going to say to them that they cannot let these wage rates go into effect. That is a matter for them, once they establish their standards and criteria.

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, what if the Pay Board adopts standards that the Cost of Living Council does not like? Would it override it? Would it request the resignation of the Members of the Pay Board? 

That is the key issue, it seems.

SECRETARY CONNALLY: I don't think it is a key issue at all, if you permit me to disagree with you for a moment.

We approach it from a completely different standpoint. We approach it from the standpoint that, first, the interest of the working people of this Country is best served by holding down inflation so that whatever increases they get as a result of their labors and their productivity increases will, in effect, be real increases, and paid in real value. 

So that there is no divergence in objective; there is no difference in our approach. 

Obviously, the people that are going to serve on this Pay Board are going to be reasonable people; intelligent people who have a sense of responsibility for making a system like this work. So I don't anticipate we are going to run into this. I don't think it is going to arise. 

Now, if I can draw an extreme position by simply saying: Let's assume that the Price Commission permitted prices that patently were exorbitant in terms of achieving the goal. Let's assume the Pay Board, on the face of it, just established a standard and criteria and announced their own goals of a 6% rate of inflation, instead of a 2% or a 3% rate. Well, at that point, we would lock horns.

So that you can't-I can think of a conceivable situation where the President would want to have something to say about what they were doing, because the Cost-of-Living Council, as I said, is going to have an over-view. 

But I don't assume that is going to happen. I assume just the opposite. Now, they are going to make the case decisions-case by case. We won't know for several months, probably, whether or not the decisions that they are making on the individual cases will indeed produce the desired results. We will be studying it. We will be watching it as we go along; but there is no desire on our part-none, whatever-there is no intention on our part to, ¶ 8393

first, give the authority and the responsibility to the Pay Board and the Price Commission, and to withhold it. We don't intend to do it. Frankly, we don't intend to do it. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, you set a goal for the rate of inflation, but not for unemployment. 

Why not? 

What do you expect the rate of unemployment to be by the end of 1972?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: Well, we certainly expect it to be lower than it is today. We have not set a goal for it, although, as you know, the goal of this Administration has been two-fold for months; in simplified form: 

No. 1: To stop the rate of inflation. 

No. 2: To bring down the rate of unemployment.

It has dropped a little bit last month, to 6%. It has dropped one-tenth of one percent. That is nothing, frankly, to crow about. It is still too high, but with the on-going Stabilization Program which the President announced last night; with the tax measures that we have pending in the Congress, on which 

I testified yesterday before the Senate Finance Committee; with other actions in the Government, we have every reason to hope-every reason, really, to believe that we are going to provide the economic expansion, the vitality, the growth, that will create the jobs. We estimate that this overall package will create between 500,000 and a million jobs. 

So that we think it is reasonable to assume that the rate of unemployment will decline during 1972.

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, the President touched only briefly on international matters.

Could you tell us when we will get to 

Phase Two of the Import Surcharge Program? 

SECRETARY CONNALLY: Well, I don't know what Phase Two of the Import Surcharge Program is, unless you mean the lifting of it. If that is what you allude to, I can't answer that any more than I can answer what the duration of the Stabilization Program on the domestic front is. It is going to continue so long as it is necessary to bring the rate of inflation under control. 

When we set a goal of 2% to 3% by the end of '72, we don't expect to end there. We expect to decline thereafter. 

Now, the international front, again: I think we are making some progress. It is not something that I am prepared to announce today; but I think we had a very good meeting of the International Monetary Fund. We had a great many private conferences with Finance Ministers of different Nations around the world. I think they recognize our problem; we recognize theirs. It is not an easy problem. It is a very difficult problem, for the simple reason that we want our balance-of-payments improved. The only way they will be improved, in a sense is to the detriment of other Nations. Other 

Nations have to give up something in order that we might gain something. 

So it is never easy to get a Nation to give up something that they have, and we have been running a deficit for 22 years in our balance-of-payments. This means other Countries have been running surpluses. 

We finally said to them, "Now, this is fine. Turn about is fair play. We have to run a surplus for a while, or, at least, break even." 

¶ 8393

That means they cannot run the surpluses they have been running. When you come down to a Nation making this kind of a decision—a political decision that this entails, it is tough for them to do. 

I think the atmosphere for negotiations with them is excellent. I think some progress, unquestionably, will be made. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, there are pending before any number of State and Federal regulatory agencies, hundreds of millions-perhaps billions of dollars worth of rate increases for telephone companies, natural gas companies, heaven only knows what other kinds of utilities. 

In view of what you said, do these Federal and State regulatory agencies, once again, have the power to act on these things, or is this something that the 

Price Board is going to work on?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: No, not unless the Price Commission gives them that authority. The Price Commission has that authority. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Sir, who is screening these appointees that are coming up before these Boards?

Are they being screened on conflict of interest, or philosphy on inflation, and security reasons?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: I must say, Sarah, a lot of us are screening them. A great many people are in on the discussions. Obviously, you try to find people who have a background and knowledge of the respective fields in which they are going to operate. We try to get the most competent people we can; people we think have a capacity both for understanding the problem, and having the courage to face up to it; having the basic objectivity to be fair in their deliberations.

The conflict of interest matter is a matter of concern and, as a consequence, any full-time employee of the Federal Government immediately subjects himself to the conflict of interest question. So that the only full-time members of the Pay Board and the Price Commission will be the Chairmen. So that the conflict of interest question is not raised. 

If you attempted to make all of the members full-time members, and subject them to conflict of interest, you would indeed have difficulty getting Labor leaders, and Business leaders, very frankly, to serve on these Boards. 

So this question does not arise in the light of the structure of the Boards themselves.

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Connally, do you expect George 

Meany will be on the Board? 

Is he going to be asked? 

Has he been asked? 

Has he refused?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: Do I expect him to be? 

I hope he will be. 

Has he been asked? 

I am not sure. If he has not, I am sure he will be. 

Has he refused? 

Not to my knowledge. ¶ 8393

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Has he accepted? 

SECRETARY CONNALLY: Not to my knowledge. I certainly hope he would.

The President talked to him on a number of occasions. I have been in a couple of meetings where he was present-where we were present together. 

They, obviously, will speak for themselves about their attitude and participation.

I would like to again say that we basically know the approach that Mr. 

Meany has. He does not want to control the Congress. Neither does the 

President. None of us do.

We want to work ourselves out of a very difficult situation as quickly as we can. At the same time, Mr. Meany has the interest of his members and the working people in this Country at heart. I cannot imagine, with the structure that is being developed here, that he could not make a great contribution to the working people of this Country and, unquestionably, his presence on the Board would contribute a very great deal to the success and the voluntary compliance that is going to have to be a part of the success of this whole operation. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: At what point would you and the COLC 

determine whether the Pay Board's decisions are in consonance with the 

President's objectives themselves?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: Well, I cannot answer that. I don't know at what point.

I start off with the basic assumption that the Members of the Pay Board and the Price Commission are going to do everything in their power to try to set standards and criteria to govern their own activities that will, indeed, produce the goal of a declining rate of inflation in this Country. 

Now, I believe that there is not any person going on either one of those Boards that is not an absolutely sincere, well intentioned American citizen; who hasn't as much commitment to this goal as any of the rest of us. 

I don't anticipate that we are ever going to have to come in conflict with them and, consequently, I have given no thought to it at all. I would not even attempt now to say under what circumstances. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, just to follow up on that, may I ask: You said a little while ago that if, after several months of decision, you decide that the Pay Board and the Price Commission do not, in fact, move in the direction of the 2% to 3% labor increase: that, at that point, you will move in.

Now, if you do, what will happen to the pay increases already asked for, or granted?

What will happen to the prices already promulgated? 

SECRETARY CONNALLY: I am not going to respond to that question. 

I want to point out that I was merely trying to say that I can conceive of a circumstance under which the President, through the Cost of Living Council, would inject himself and the Government back into these decisions if, indeed, they got completely out of hand. But I don't anticipate that that is going to happen.

The point I am trying to make is that the Government is not divorcing itself from the solution of this problem. 

¶ 8393

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, you said that the goal is to get inflation down to 2% to 3% by the end of '72.

What will have to be accomplished before the program will be terminated? 

SECRETARY CONNALLY: I think there will have to be a basic agreement and feeling throughout the Country that the inflationary psychology has been halted and has been broken, and that there is in this Country a commitment to stability; to price stability; to wage stability; so that we can know what to expect in terms of the future. We have been going several years with inflation, and the anticipation of inflation, as an integral part of economic activities in this Country. It has reached the point where we cannot abide it any more. We have to stop it. 

Now, I can't tell you what month and what day we will reach the point where we have, indeed, erased from the minds of people that they are living in a Society where there is going to be nothing but continuing inflation. 

We want to reach the point-we have to reach the point—where the people understand that they can experience, and that they can hope to expect, stability in this economic system. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, there has been considerable activity by the Council in the area of employee benefits. 

I am wondering whether the new Pay Board will be expected to use these rulings in setting up their plans for fringe benefits, or can they start from fresh?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: The rulings of the Cost of Living Council will remain in effect until they are changed or altered by the Pay Board.

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, the economy of this Coun try apparently is to be divided, for the purpose of this new phase, into three parts:

Those units that will have to advise in advance, a proposed wage or price increase; 

Those that can report later;

Those that are spot-checked. 

My first inquiry is: Who is going to be in each category?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: The Price Commission is going to deter mine that.

The point to which Mr. Schorr refers is the division, into three categories, of economic interest: (1) The category representing the largest economic units in the Country that will be required to file a pre-notification of any price or wage change. 

This will, obviously, be the largest economic units in the Country. How many, I don't know.

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: It is a matter of size, rather than the type of industry?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: Probably, but this is something, again, that the Price Commission will have to refine. 

Then there will be a second group that will not have to pre-notify in the event of a price change, but will be in what we call a "reporting category". 

They will have to periodically file reports of what prices they actually charge, and wages they pay, and so forth. ¶ 8393

The third group will be, probably, the largest, in terms of numbers of entities, and numbers of businesses. I would relate these to the corner grocery store type of operation, where they don't have to pre-notify, or report, on any periodic basis but, rather, they will have to keep adequate records. They would have the same rules applied to them, but they just would not have to report, or notify; but they would be subject to spot check by the Compliance-Inspection and Compliance Division -and they would be subject to the same rules and regulations, the same standards and criteria that everybody else is. It would just be a different mechanism of enforcement.

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: May I ask a clarification question on that same thing, please?

Will wages also follow that same three-part thing, that if certain firms want to

SECRETARY CONNALLY (Interposing) If I said "wages," I should MEMBER OF THE PRESS: No. I am asking, for example, if General 

Motors wants to increase wages, which might push inflation, do they have to request permission in advance? not have.

SECRETARY CONNALLY: I believe they would. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Then wages would also be covered under the three-part thing?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: Yes. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, from your experience in 

Government, what makes you think that a structure, as complicated as this, will work?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: Well, everything is relative. I think this is fairly simple. There is no great Bureaucracy. We anticipate that this whole program will be run by approximately 3,000 people. 

All you have here involved is a Pay Board that is going to make decisions with respect to wages, salaries, and fringe benefits. Fifteen people are going to make this decision. They are going to have a relatively small staff; probably 100 people. 

You are going to have a Price Commission of seven people; all Public 

Members. They are going to make the basic decision with respect to prices. 

You are going to have a Public Board dealing with interest and dividends. 

They are going to make those decisions. I don't think it is complicated. I think it is all very simple. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Are you not going to have thousands of contested decisions that some Solomon is going to have to eventually decide? 

SECRETARY CONNALLY: You obviously are going to have questions. 

You obviously are going to have requests for exemptions. There is no question about that. But, again, part of these problems can be resolved by the establishment of the standards and criteria to begin with, so that everyone 

1 knows what the rules are.

This is why the President has given these two Boards 37 days. This is why he made his announcement as early as he possibly could, in order to get 

¶ 8393

these Boards constituted; get them on board; get them functioning; get their standards and criteria developed before they become effective on November 14. 

Sure, there are going to be requests for exemptions. I don't know any way around that, but I think if the people basically understand what the objectives are, that our experience during the Freeze period has indicated that it is going to amaze you how few complaints, and how few difficulties, you really have.

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: I would like to ask two questions, Mr. Secretary.

First, consistent with your goal on inflation, what would you say would be the maximum permissible pay increase? 

Would it be about 5% or 52% a year?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: I would not attempt to assign any maximum amount to any particular wage increase, or any particular wage contract. 

In the first place, it won't be my business. It is the business of the Pay 

Board to decide that. 

In the second place, it will depend on how many people are affected. 

It depends on what the equity is. 

It depends on whether or not their peculiar situation requires a small, or a large, increase in order to bring them into an equitable position with their counterparts in the economy.

So there are many factors that have to be considered. 

I am not about to assign a precise figure on the amount of the increase that could be given, because I think it would be, in the first place, wrong. 

I think you can expect, now, that the Pay Board might well, indeed, permit some fairly large increases, but to the extent that they grant large ones, they are going to have to hold down on somebody. Others will have to be smaller.

So, no: You cannot look to any one wage contract and determine whether or not the program is working, or is failing. You cannot do that. It is going to have to be an average. And, of course, a lot of it is going to depend on productivity itself. How much productivity are we going to achieve? This will have a large part in determining what kind of wage increases there can be in this Country.

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: The second question: 

If your Price Commission determines that some company is making a windfall profit, what power does it have?

Legally, how does it go about forcing that company to pay that back through lower prices?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: It is going to be given the power to roll back prices; actually roll prices back to achieve that objective. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Do you suppose, sir, that Mr. Meany and the other labor leaders who may be on the Pay Board will adequately reflect the interest of the working men of America? 

SECRETARY CONNALLY: I think they will certainly try. I don't know anybody better, to do it. ¶ 8393 ©

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, can you tell me whether or not there is going to be any liaison between the Pay Board and the Price Board?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: Basically, it will be coordinated on major policy matters at the Cost of Living Council level, just to be sure there is a basic balance between the two. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: To avoid a wage/price spiral, Mr. Secre tary: let's suppose one Union wins a fairly large increase. The Company then comes in and asks for a price increase to justify that. 

How would you manage to sit on that? 

SECRETARY CONNALLY: I don't want to get into specific cases about what is going to happen, but I assume that neither will be operating in a vacuum. Both will be informed about what is happening in the other. They are two very small groups. They are all going to know each other. Part of their responsibility, obviously, is going to be working in tandem, even though they work in different fields, to achieve the desired objectives. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: What do you plan to do about the other side of inflation? That is, the reduction of quality in goods and services.

SECRETARY CONNALLY: Well, I would hope that the American workmen and the American businessman would not think that it was in their long term interest to try to cheat on the quality of the products that they produce. I cannot imagine that there are going to be many people in this 

Country that take that type of an attitude. 

The answer is: I don't know of anything we are going to do, except that the Price Commission, again, has the responsibility and the authority to determine prices and, obviously, they can do so in terms of the quality of the commodity, or the product. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, interest rates are made up, in part, of inflationary expectations. If you succeed, and you get inflation down to a rate of about 3%, is it reasonable to expect interest rates to drop by 3%?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: Yes. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: And, if they don't, would you then use the stand-by authority you are requesting, to move against them?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: I would certainly assume that a part of the high interest rates that we have been experiencing in this Country in the last couple of years are at least partially the result of anticipated inflation, and that if we can convince the American people-and this includes the moneylending institutions-that there is going to be an end to this inflationary spiral, that it will have a very pronounced effect upon interest rates. If, indeed, it does not, then the Commission on Interest and Dividends will have the authority to do something about it. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, is this stand-by authority on interest rates and dividends the reason you are going to ask the Congress to extend the Economic Stabilization Act until 1973? Or do you think it is going to take that long to turn the American public's feeling about inflation around?

¶ 8393

SECRETARY CONNALLY: We certainly want the authority-the 

President does-beyond its expiration date of April 30, 1972. So we have to ask for an extension of a year, in any event. 

In so doing, he has already asked the bi-partisan leadership for that extension and for the additional power-stand-by power-to control interest and dividends. 

Now, this does not indicate that we think, necessarily, that all of the objectives will be achieved within that time period. I would hope they would. 

None of us want to prolong these controls.

Frankly, the Stabilization Program on which we will enter is a way station to the goal of achieving an acceptable rate of inflation of 2% to 3% by the end of the year, and declining thereafter, and returning this economy to the free market.

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, the President, last night, said he was gratified that other Nations now understand the American view that foreign trade should be "fair," as well as "free."

Does this suggest that maybe you are making some definite progress in consultation with other Countries for them to dismantle their barriers against 

American goods?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: Yes. I think we can expect that, over the next several months, we will see an elimination, either on a unilateral basis, or as a result of bi-lateral negotiations, of certain restrictions and trade barriers that presently exist.

Now, let me point out that it has never been a part of our objectives, in terms of solving the international monetary problems that now exist, to require an overall comprehensive GATT type of arrangement with respect to trade matters, but there are certain specific changes and corrections-if I can use that word-that, frankly, I think we can go about in a very brief period of time. I think we can look forward to achieving some of those goals. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, this background paper that 

I have here says that: Controls of particular sectors may be removed when the action is consistent with the general objectives of the program. 

Does this mean that one or more industries may be exempt before the overall program is terminated entirely? 

SECRETARY CONNALLY: It is entirely possible. It depends on what the Price Commission and the Pay Board determine they are justified in doing. It is entirely possible that they can begin relaxing the controls at some relatively early time. But that, again, is a matter for them to decide. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, do you anticipate the 

Committee on Interests and Dividends will have guidelines, also, in 37 days? 

If so, how would these be enforced?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: I don't anticipate they will, necessarily, have guidelines. I don't think it is as essential that they do, for two reasons: 

First, we have had, as you well know, remarkable success in getting voluntary compliance with respect to restraints on dividends, even though we had no statutory authority to control dividends. 

We have, by the process of requesting cooperation, been able to restrain increases in dividends. So we don't anticipate this will be any problem of major significance, whatsoever. ¶ 8393

With respect to interest rates: During the Freeze period, as the President said when he made his speech on August 15, we anticipated that the mere establishment of the Freeze itself would result in interest rates coming down. 

And they have, indeed, come down.

Let me, in this connection, give you just a few figures, because I think this is important. 

Interest rates on Treasury bills for three months, since August 13—on 

August 13, they were 5.15%. 

On October 7, they were down to 4.56%.

This is a drop of 59 basis points-over a 10% drop. 

The six-month bills are down 76 basis points. That looks like a 15% drop.

I am just mentally making these percentage calculations here. 

But it is a drop of 5.51% to 4.75%. 

So on, down the list.

In every single category-1-year, 3-years, 7-years; 10-years-Treasury coupons; Federal Bonds, 1-year; 3-years; 3-year Federal Bonds down 7.3 to 

6.20. That is a drop of 1.12 basis points, which is about a 16% drop. So, in every single category, interest rates have gone down. I don't anticipate this is going to be a major problem. One of the reasons why-I am not sure-we certainly cannot promulgate standards; we may be developing them in our staff work, except, of course, we may not have the authority-we certainly hope we will-before the 14th. But the extension of the Stabilization Act will carry with it the statutory stand-by authority for interest and dividends. I would certainly hope we would have that from the Congress by the 14th. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, a couple of questions about enforcement.

First of all, I understand that the Chairman of the Board or Commission will have the power to seek lawsuits from the Justice Department. 

SECRETARY CONNALLY: That is correct. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Will they be able to do this only with the approval of the majority of their respective Board or Commission? And, conversely, could they do it if the majority of the Board or Commission does not want them to institute lawsuits?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: Well, I would assume they certainly would be bound by this question. This question has not been raised, as to what procedures they would set up. I would assume they would have to have a majority vote of their Board or Commission in order to seek Court action through the Department of Justice.

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Second question, sir. 

Can the Cost of Living Council initiate legal action against violators of the standards that are set?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: We could have, and will have, contemporaneous authority with the Pay Board and the Price Commission to ask for sanctions against offenders. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, let me ask you a question -perhaps ask for a specific definition and, maybe, an example of what a windfall profit would be?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: Well, a windfall profit in general terms, as best I can define it for you, is a profit that, basically, has its origin out of 

¶ 8393

the operation of the controls themselves. It is not a profit that arises from efficiency of management, or sale of assets, or things of that sort. 

A windfall profit is, basically and generally defined, at least in my mind, as a profit that results from the operation of the control program. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, what will be the status of the Construction Industry Stabilization Committee-if you can tell us—in this post-freeze period? 

Will it continue to operate as it does now?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: Yes, sir. It will continue to operate as it does now, under the jurisdiction of the Pay Board.

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, is 37 days a realistic figure to allow Boards, that have not been publicly set up, time to determine all of the case loads that must be on the books now? 

SECRETARY CONNALLY: It is a world of time! It is a world of time! 

When I consider what we went through in the Cost of Living Council, when we were hit with the Freeze on August 15, and the progress that was made in a two-week period of time, it is incredible what you can accomplish, really, when people really get down and get to work; and I know that this 

Pay Board and the Price Commission will do so; and I think they do have ample time. It is not going to be easy. They are going to have to work, but there is, certainly ample time.

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, would your definition of 

"windfall" cover the wage increases that were contracted for, that Labor has not been getting during the Freeze, and any proportion of those which they might not get under the "fall,” that money goes into the treasuries of corporations as a result of the program, doesn't it? 

SECRETARY CONNALLY: It might well do it. 

Now, let me make clear that I am not talking about trying to identify the flow of every dollar for every purpose into and out of a corporation, but I think the Price Commission will have the authority, where they think there have been windfall profits-I can give you no more definition than I have given you-but they have the authority; and will be looking at the profits of corporations that they think might have been generated, or increased, as the result of the operation of this program; in which case, they are going to be asked and empowered to roll back the prices so that the consumers of this country can share in these benefits. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: And a like question, Mr. Secretary: What happens to the dividends that are voluntarily held back very successfully under the voluntary restraint?

Doesn't that accumulate within the corporations, to be paid at a later date?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: Well, it might. 

They might not pay it. They might modernize their plant and equipment. 

There is a shortage of capital. It is significant that the average age of equip ment in the industrial complex of America has gone up to the point where, today, 44% of all of the equipment in the industrial complex, is 10 years or older. This is up from 35%, just about six years ago. So it may well be that they will take a lot of that money and reinvest it in modernized equipment so they can be more competitive in the world markets. We hope that this will be one of the results. ¶ 8393

While we are on this question of profits, let me point out to you that profits have been unusually low this year, and last year; that, as of today, profits in terms of Gross National Product are the lowest they have been since 1938. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, would stepped-up anti-trust prosecution be a part of Phase Two, or would the controls make this, perhaps, less necessary?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: I think it would make it less necessary and, very frankly, this matter has not been discussed at all. I would assume that the very aggressive attitude that Dick McLaren, in the Anti-Trust Division, constantly manifests, will be continued. I have not seen any lessening of it. 

I am sure they will not diminish their effort. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, you set up a special com mittee to handle the rising cost of medical care. 

Who will have the majority vote on that?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: This will be on an Advisory group basis, simply because medical costs have been such—it is an identifiable segment of the American economy where the costs have gone up just tremendously and so the Committee on Medical Services Industries will actually be an Advisory group. They will not have the authority to make decisions. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, there are, obviously, some industries some major industries—that are going to get special attention because of their effect on prices. 

SECRETARY CONNALLY: I am sure they won't like it, but they will probably get some special attention. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Can you tell us who some of these un happy industries are going to be, just in general terms?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: No. No. I cannot, because I don't want to anticipate what either the Price Commission, or the Pay Board are going to do. 

Now when you, a moment ago, alluded-as I recall,-in response to a question by Mr. Schorr, to the fact there is going to be a group in the prenotification category-I assume this is the group to which you alluded. Obviously, this is going to be composed of the largest, the biggest, and the strongest economic units in the Country. You know who they are better than I do. 

They know who they are!-That is the important part. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Secretary, the legal authority for the 

Stabilization Program rests with the Economic Stabilization Act, which expires on April 30.

Do you anticipate any problem with Congress in extending it? 

If Congress does not extend it, what, then, will happen? 

SECRETARY CONNALLY: Well, let me answer the first part of that question or the first question-and I hope it will answer the second. 

I don't anticipate any great trouble in the Congress. In the briefing that the President had with the bi-partisan leaders yesterday afternoon at the White House, I thought the reaction to the President's proposed program was very good. I thought they manifested, on both sides of the aisle, a spirit of 

¶ 8393

cooperation and a willingness to help, to do their part, as every American is being asked to do his part in this continuing fight against inflation. 

I don't anticipate any trouble at all.

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: It is not for me, not being a “regular” in 

Treasury, to bring this conference to a close. 

SECRETARY CONNALLY: I would appreciate it, Mr. Schorr, if you would!

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: It is, at least, my final question. 

The way you are working yourself, as you are, into this great establishment, do you think you can possibly be spared by the President for possibly other political duties?

SECRETARY CONNALLY: I would hope not! 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Thank you, Mr. Secretary.

Text of October 12, 1971 press conference of George P. Shultz, Director, Office of Management and Budget. 

MR. SHULTZ: Any questions, gentlemen?

Q. Mr. Shultz, precisely what power does the President and/or the Cost of Living Council now retain?

MR. SHULTZ: Both the President and the Cost of Living Council, acting in his behalf, as his statement said the statement that organized labor had and which you had and others have had as we have distributed them—the Cost of Living Council has the responsibility for the overall operation of the program, looking at what the Pay Board does, what the Price Commission does, what happens in interests and rents, how successful we are in working out something in the medical area and so on and articulating these together, so that is one principal responsibility of the Cost of Living Council and, of course, it has the responsibility in the areas of enforcement, surveillance and general informational activity as part of the field organization. 

Q. In one of the statements you point out the function of the Cost of 

Living Council as serving as a policy review group which would concern itself with the pattern and impact as to achieve stated goals and objectives. 

MR. SHULTZ: The Pay Board will set criteria and judge cases so it will move along in its work. The Price Commission will do the same thing. It will set criteria and judge cases according to those criteria and move along in its work.

The Committee on Interest and Dividends will do the same. The Cost of Living Council will look at the results of all that, think about the criteria, ask itself if these are compatible with each other and most important, if they are compatible with the overall goal which is stated in this memorandum and which I think is broadly accepted as a desirable goal, that is, to get the rate of inflation down to two or three percent by the end of 1972. 

And so we will be asking: Are we getting there? Are we on the track?

Are we making progress and if not, what can we do about it? 

Q. Supposing they are not compatible? ¶ 8394

MR. SHULTZ: We don't expect that will be the case, but if it is, we will try to discuss it, work it out as reasonable people working together. If the whole thing gets completely off the track, of course, the President can just abolish the machinery and try something else. 

But I think there has been so much nitpicking about precisely what is this relationship going to be and that relationship going to be that we tend to lose sight of the fact that the important thing is a cooperative spirit among reasonable people trying to solve a problem that they share and [ac]knowledge, that is what we are trying to develop and I think we are a long step in that direction today as a result of all the things that have happened. 

Q. Mr. Shultz, Mr. Meany said in his news conference today that he thought the program would be a success if it reached a goal of four percent inflation by the end of 1972.

Does that mean that there is a conflict at the outset here? 

MR. SHULTZ: Well, all I can refer you to is the summary statement which the President went over yesterday and initialed. Our goal is to get the rate of inflation to the two to three percent level by the end of 1972 or sooner, if possible.

I think by our measurement of the Consumer Price Index, our measurement of the GNP deflator that we are somewhere near four percent now. The question is can we get it down further. 

I might say that is by way of saying there has been headway against the rate of inflation and it is because things are moving in the right direction that programs of this kind have a chance to succeed. 

In most of the cases where things have been tried, what you have had is a situation where things were out of control and getting worse and then something is put in there to stop it and most of the time it has proven futile. 

Here because the environment is different and because we think we can keep the fiscal monetary environment different we have a chance of succeeding in furthering the progress which has already been made. 

Q. On Friday, Secretary Connally said on November 14 he would consider the freeze extended with exception granted by the Pay Board and Price 

Commission. Today Mr. Meany said as of November 14 he would consider all contracts unfrozen. 

Is there a difference here? 

MR. SHULTZ: No, the Cost of Living Council will, so to speak, hand the freeze to the Pay Board and the Price Commission and the Committee on Interest and Dividends, assuming they are organized and have developed their work procedures and so on. When that happens, what kind of standards you go by on deferred increases or new contract negotiations, or whatever, will be under the criteria established by the Pay Board or the Price Commission. 

But I think it is important to emphasize that as a transitional proposition. 

Q. When is the President going to name the members of these Boards?

MR. SHULTZ: As soon as we can now get them lined up and we are working on that and have got a number of names under consideration and we expect to move very promptly on it. 

Q. Has anyone refused to serve so far? 

MR. SHULTZ: Oh, we have explored with a number of people, some are really not particularly interested, others are, and we are trying to get ourselves positioned to line up these Boards finally.

THE PRESS: Thank you, Mr. Shultz.

Text of October 15, 1971 press conference of Donald Rumsfeld, Counsellor to the President and Frank Carlucci, Associate Director, Office of Management and Budget.

MR. ZIEGLER: The President today is issuing an Executive Order providing for the stabilization of prices, rents, wages and salaries. You have a Fact Sheet and a copy of that Executive Order. 

I would like to call your attention to Point No. 5 in the Fact Sheet where it states that the Executive Order provides for a new Director of the Cost of Living Council, and goes on to say that this position will be filled by Mr. 

Donald Rumsfeld, until recently Counsellor to the President. That should be changed to read: "The position will be filled by Donald Rumsfeld, a 

Counsellor to the President." Mr. Rumsfeld will continue with his responsibilities as a Counsellor to the President and a Member of the Cabinet when he assumes his additional responsibilities as Director of the Cost of Living Council.

Mr. Rumsfeld is here this morning to discuss the Executive Order with you, together with Frank Carlucci, Associate Director of the Office of Management and Budget.

You have had a brief time to look over the Executive Order and the Fact 

Sheet. With that, I will present to you Don Rumsfeld. 

MR. RUMSFELD: Thank you. The document you have before you, or the Executive Order and the delegation agreements, in effect accomplish what the President announced on October 10th insofar as his role in it goes. They will create the Pay Board, the Price Commission, the various boards on health, State and local government, and the Committee on Interest and Dividends. 

Following this up, of course, will be the legislation which will go up the early part of next week. I will he happy to respond to questions. 

Q. Mr. Rumsfeld, on a quick reading of the Executive Order and Order 4,

Delegation of Authority, I don't find anything either repeating or seeming to implement the statement and the summary of the role of the Cost of Living Council and the Pay Board and Price Commission issued last Tuesday, the one that said the Council will not approve, advise or vote or veto the actions of the Pay Board.

MR. RUMSFELD: The answer is that it is consistent with that and that is, in effect, what the Executive Order and Delegation Agreements do is, insofar as legal and technical language is required, it sets out the relationship. 

The specific and more detailed comments that were initialed by the President are in effect.

Q. One follow-up question, the Executive Order and the Delegation of 

Authority to the Pay Board, does that continue the power of review that the original White House background paper said the Cost of Living would have? 

MR. RUMSFELD: The answer to that is the same as the other one.

The paper that was circulated and signed by the President is in effect and that sets forth the details as to the relationships between the Cost of Living Council and the Price Commission and the Pay Board. 

Q. Why are we not getting the legislation today?

MR. RUMSFELD: The legislation is, as I understand it, completed. 

It is in the process of consultation with the appropriate Congressional committees and will be put forward to the Congress early in the week. ¶ 8395

When do you expect to have the Members of the Pay Board and the 

Price Commission named?

MR. RUMSFELD: I would think in the next several days we would have the names of the Price Commission and Pay Board. 

Q. What is the cause of the delay?

MR. RUMSFELD: No particular event or problem. It is just a matter of discussing the matter with the individuals involved and ascertaining the extent to which they can change their schedules and arrange to serve. The vast majority of the work is completed and it should be hopefully concluded sometime next week at the latest. 

Q. Are you getting a lot of turn-downs? 

MR. RUMSFELD: Not to my knowledge, no.

Q. The health industry is singled out in a unique matter, why was that and would you give me some examples of the special consideration you might see coming up.

MR. RUMSFELD: The answer to that, I think, was covered by the 

President in his remarks of October 7, if I recall correctly. In effect, it was felt that this was an area that was important to the economy as a whole, to be dealt with in a way that involved people from that particular sector and that it would be helpful to create a group such as this Board to advise the particular Commissions and Boards that have the responsibility for it. 

It is complicated. There is legislation pending. And it was felt that that would be useful. It will be advisory.

Q. What are some of the special considerations that are mentioned in your fact sheet here? 

MR. RUMSFELD: Well, the question of special considerations in the health area is not terribly dissimilar from that in the state and local govern- ment area. What you have is two big sectors that involve a variety of different groups that relate to a good deal of federal activity, some of which is in place, some of which is being proposed or scheduled for change in the Congress and that kind of advice like the Productivity Commission's advice, is useful. 

Q. Mr. Rumsfeld, we have been told that the function of the Cost of 

Living Council, among other things, is to see that the standards and criteria and actions of the Pay Board and Price Commission are in consonance with the thought objectives of the President.

As the man on the line, how would you interpret that or more specifically, how would you implement that?

MR. RUMSFELD: I don't think it needs a good deal of interpretation. 

The President, in effect, by this Executive Order, is continuing the Cost of Living Council. As he indicated in that statement he initialed, it is desired that there would be this group to see that the various elements of the President's proposal actually operate in harmony and make sense one with the other.

Secondly, the President has set out a general goal, a sensible goal, a goal that has obviously received the support of the overwhelming majority of the American people, and the role of the Council will be to see what progress can be made towards reaching that goal, as opposed to handling specific cases or appeals.

¶ 8395

Q. The apparent difference is to whether the inflation goal is two to three percent or two to four percent of this. 

MR. RUMSFELD: There is no confusion or controversy over it, to my knowledge. The President indicated in his remarks that he wanted to reduce the pressure on the increases in the cost of living. The Cost of Living Council has subsequently indicated that it would like to set as a goal a reduction by five percent of the present rate by the end of 1972. That is the framework within which this program has been developed and certainly represents the best judgments of the President and the Cost of Living Council. 

Q. Mr. Rumsfeld, do you expect to have the Medical Cost Board, the 

State and Local Government Board and the Interest Committee named at the same time as the Pay Board and the Price Commission are named, or will there be further delay in that? 

MR. RUMSFELD: First of all, let me put your question in the proper framework. The President made his announcement on the post-freeze period many weeks in advance of the November 13 date which is the end of the Phase 1 period. The reason he did that was because the period in between the two was to be used for exactly what it is being used for, the development of the Executive Order, Delegation agreements, selection of individuals to serve on these Boards.

It is going forward in a very orderly process. People understand that the freeze remains in effect. There is no confusion about this, to my knowledge, and it seems to me that it is going along apace. 

Now in specific answer to your question, my best guess would be that the 

Health and State and Local Government Advisory Boards would follow the creation and appointment of individuals to the Pay Board and Price Commission. This Executive Order provides for their establishment; it also provides for the Committee on Interest and Dividends, which Arthur Burns will chair, that is being established by Burns under this Executive Order and it will be very prompt. 

Q. Will that be an all-government board? 

MR. RUMSFELD: The answer is yes to the extent you look at the names of the individuals assigned and they are all officially government; legally, yes. 

Q. We were told last week by a government briefer that there would be no Senate confirmation process for Members of the Pay Board and Price Commission; does that still stand?

MR. RUMSFELD: Yes, this Executive Order creates the Pay Board and Price Commission and the Economic Stabilization Act gives the President authority to appoint these individuals. As I say, they will be appointed. You cannot confirm an individual until the Congress creates a position to be confirmed for. It is important that these individuals gather next week and begin to do the very important work the President has assigned them. 

Q. How many persons have been asked to serve and how many have turned it down and what in general have been the reasons for turning the job down? 

MR. RUMSFELD: I have not been involved in that process and I cannot answer the question. The only ones I have heard of have been individuals who recognize that it will take a major time commitment on their part and for personal reasons felt their circumstances would not allow such a time commitment. ¶ 8395

Q. Did any say they disagreed with the basic philosophy of the program? 

MR. RUMSFELD: Not to my knowledge.

Q. The current Economic Stabilization Act only gives the President authority to set guidelines in the construction industry. If the Pay Board would like to set industry guidelines, do they need Congressional approval for other industries or can the Pay Board set the guidelines independently? 

MR. RUMSFELD: We have an attorney here, Mr. Simms, from the 

Office of Management and Budget. 

MR. SIMMS: The goals can be set by the Council and then under these goals of the Council, the Pay Board and Price Commission will be able to set their own criteria or guidelines on any basis that they want to. 

Q. But the Congress said that you would have to prove a gross disproportionate wage. 

MR. SIMMS: If you dealt only with one industry, and at the time of the construction industry that was the only one covered, but now everything is covered under the Order.

Now, if you wanted to exempt everything except one industry, maybe you have to make a similar finding. 

Q. Mr. Rumsfeld, is it the intention that the Pay Board and Price Commission will, before the time, the date, that the current 'freeze expires, issue a general guideline or indication of the base point on which wages or price increases can be calculated or will they do it all case by case? 

MR. RUMSFELD: I would not want to prejudge exactly what they will do. It is clear to the people of the country that the freeze remains in effect until something happens by these groups to alter that. Presumably they will meet and make judgments as to how they feel we can best handle the postfreeze period.

I would doubt that they would operate in favor of only dealing with individual cases. I would think they would develop guidelines to handle it. 

Q. About the timing, will they try to reach a base line point before the freeze expires? 

MR. RUMSFELD: I don't think it is really useful for me to try and guess what they will do.

Q. Will there be an appeal body set up for decisions by these boards? 

MR. RUMSFELD: The legislation will deal with that. 

Q. In regard to the functions of the Boards and Commissions, the President uses the word "delegate" in referring to the Council's relationship to those two Boards. Why did he use that phrase and why was he not more explicit as to what their functioning will be as he has been in his speeches? 

MR. RUMSFELD: I guess the reason is that the Executive Order is an instrument to be used for some things and to the extent that additional instruments are needed, the Delegation Agreements serve that purpose. That is why we released both documents simultanenously, the Executive Order and 

Delegation Agreements. 

Q. What are you telling people who ask you about the use of alternates on this Board-are you saying they can use them or can't? 

MR. RUMSFELD: I have not been approached with this question.

Q. Has the question come up and what is the view of the Administration on alternates? 

MR. RUMSFELD: I would estimate that what would happen would be there would be other procedural questions such as that, that would have to be addressed by the Commission and the Board. They will, at some point, consult with the Cost of Living Council about it. 

Q. Can you clarify on page two the reference to "Whether by retroactive increase or otherwise?" What meaning has that? That is in the Executive

Order. Does that rule out any action which would recover any of the freeze period wages or prices? What is the meaning of that phrase, "Whether by retroactive increase or otherwise." That is on page two, third paragraph, Section 1. It is the second full paragraph. Under Prices, Wages and Rents, and everything else stabilized as of August 6 and then he says, “No person shall charge, assess, or receive, directly or indirectly, pay or agree to pay in any transaction wages or salaries in any form, or to use any means to obtain payment of wages and salaries in any form, higher than those permitted hereunder, whether by retroactive increase or otherwise." 

MR. CARLUCCI: This is taken out of the existing Order. In drawing up this Order, we had to establish a base period. We had to have something from which you move. So we took the existing Order and the phrase in this section that says, "Pending action under this Order.” All of the rest of this section continues in effect. 

So that allows the existing situation to continue in effect until modified by one of the entities set up by the Executive Order. 

Q. Specifically the question is, does this prohibit the Pay and Wage 

Boards from taking any action which would recapture some of that retroactively?

MR. CARLUCCI: They are authorized in this section to modify it. 

MR. RUMSFELD: The key words are "pending action under this Order," meaning action of the Pay Board and Price Commission. 

Q. Will the legislation go up Monday? 

MR. RUMSFELD: I am not sure, as far as protocol, whether it should go up when one House is not in session. It will go up Monday or Tuesday when it is proper to do it from that standpoint. 

Q. Could not Congress insist on confirming Members of the Pay Board and Price Commission?

MR. RUMSFELD: Certainly Article 1 of the Constitution gives the 

Congress the authority to do such things. 

Q. This would not be unconstitutional for them to do that? 

MR. RUMSFELD: They can pass laws on subjects such as that. 

Q. Would the White House oppose an effort by Congress to provide for confirmation of the Chairman of the Pay Board and the Price Commission if at the same time they provided that in the interim the two bodies could get down to work on what would amount to a recess appointment? 

MR. RUMSFELD: I think that is a question that is down the road.

In fact, the President has set forward his approach and recommendation and this is what is represented here and which will be added onto by the presentation of the legislation early next week. ¶ 8395

Q. I am still trying to get clear in my mind your responses to the first couple of questions on the President's Memorandum that was given to the 

AFL-CIO Executive Council. Are you saying to us that that Memorandum has the effect of law, that is, it is a legal document? 

MR. RUMSFELD: It is not a legal document. It was not drafted by lawyers. It was drafted the way human beings work things out. In fact, I indicated that the Executive Order and Delegation Agreements are legal documents. They, in no way, conflict one with another. 

My statement was that the Memorandum which was initialed by the President remains the understanding and this material here in no way contradicts or conflicts with it. 

Q. Is there specific language in here—we have not had a chance to really read this through—which would support that understanding, is there something we can quote?

MR. RUMSFELD: Certainly. The Delegation of Authority you have there, if you read it, both the specifics and the whole, you will see that it not only is not in conflict, but is in agreement. Section 1(b), says "More particularly, the Price Commission, acting through its Chairman, shall establish criteria, standards, and implementation procedures designed to stabilize prices and rents within the general economic stabilization goals and coverage determinations developed by the Council." 

Q. But there are no "Thou Shalt Not's" with respect to the Council in this Authority. 

MR. RUMSFELD: You have to make a decision about whether saying thou shall or thou shall not. It puts it in the positive.

At the bottom of paragraph (b) it says, "Such procedures shall include ."—and it put it in the positive "but not be limited to, those necessary to, decide individual cases ..; recommend to the Department of Justice enforcement action . . .; maintain liaison . .; maintain liaison with ... the 

Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service . . ." and so forth. 

Q. Where in any of this legal material is there an inhibition or prohibition on the Cost of Living Council equivalent to the inhibition and prohibition contained in the non-legal Memorandum of the President? 

MR. RUMSFELD: What you have is what is before you. It is in every way consistent with the statement that was initialed by the President. 

Q. Except that there are omissions, is that right? 

MR. RUMSFELD: Not to my knowledge. There may be words or phrases that are not identical because one is a legal document and the other is a Memorandum of understanding.

Q. Where can you show us in this legal material the prohibitions on the 

Cost of Living Council with respect to review of the decisions of the Pay Board?

MR. CARLUCCI: The purpose of this Executive Order is just to set up these entities and get them functioning. This in no way supersedes or affects the agreement the President initialed a few days ago. It is not the responsibility of the Executive Order to describe in precise detail the relationship between every entity. It sets them up in order that they can get going and functioning. 

¶ 8395

Q. I am asking, do you acknowledge or agree with the statement that the President's Memorandum, given to the AFL-CIO Executive Council, has no legal standing?

MR. RUMSFELD: The question is one of those questions that, it seems to me, misses the point. The point is that the Cost of Living Council is created by the President. It serves the President. They understand what that Memorandum said. They have Delegation Agreements from the President and the 

Cost of Living Council to the Pay Board and Price Commission which reflect an understanding of that. 

To my knowledge, there is no set of relationships like this where every single thing in direct answer to your question is spelled out legally. Life being what it is, what we are doing here is creating something to deal with a very important problem that faces the country and there is an understanding on the part of all parties to my knowledge as to exactly what we are beginning and how that relationship is going to work. 

Q. Why did you establish some of these relationships legally and others on a non-legal basis?

Q. Doesn't Section 2 take care of that, delegating the Council's authority to the Board, to perform these functions? Isn't that saying that the Council gives up its authority on those areas to the Board? 

MR. RUMSFELD: They do. The Executive Order and Delegation 

Agreement do, but I think the fact remains that someone could find some word or phrase and say, "Well, that is not in there, but it is understood." This is the basic arrangement for the relationship. 

Q. Mr. Rumsfeld, the Cost of Living Council said in the paper issued along with the President's speech on October 7, that the Cost of Living Council could and would set and announce initial standards if the Board and the Price Commission had not had time to do so. Is that still the intention?

Q. There was nothing hypothetical in the statement of the Cost of Living supplemental paper.

Query: Would then the Cost of Living Council two days before that announce some interim arrangement?

It seems to me that that would be a decision that would have to be made by the Cost of Living Council. I would think it would not be, frankly, useful to come out with interim arrangements that would last only a matter of hours or a few days and that they would have to weigh that as to when they believe the Board and Commission would actually be able to produce their work. 

The important point is that we have every reason to believe that the Pay Board and Price Commission will meet, make some judgments with respect to this and put them forward.

Q. Mr. Rumsfeld, this may be answered in the papers which I have not had a chance to read fully, but will the decisions on the breaking down of ¶ 8395

the economy and sectors that have to report in advance, sectors that have to report periodically and sectors that don't have to report, will that breakdown be decided by the Cost of Living Council or by the Pay Board and the Price Commission?

Q. Do you have a specific deadline by which you now want those decisions you referred to a moment ago, to be made?

MR. RUMSFELD: The deadline has been announced by the President. 

The Boards will be appointed. They will meet, they will make judgments. 

They will make announcements as to what will take place at the point where the freeze is lifted. Correction, where there are changes made to the existing freeze.

As far as a specific deadline, the hope is we will achieve it prior to the expiration of the 90 days.

Delegation of Authority from CLC to the Pay Board 

¶ 8401 

Cost of Living Council Order No. 3: Delegation of Authority Concerning Stabilization of Wages and Salaries, October 15, 1971 (36 Federal Register 20202, October 15, 1971): 

Pursuant to the authority vested in the Council by Section 4 of Executive Order No. 11627 (hereinafter referred to as the Executive Order), it is hereby ordered as follows: 

1. (a) There is delegated to the Pay Board (established by section 7 of the Executive Order) acting through its Chairman, responsibility for implementing, administering, monitoring and providing for the enforcement_of the stabilization of wages and salaries in conformity with the Executive Order. (b) More particularly, the Pay Board, acting through its Chairman, shall establish criteria, standards, and implementation procedures designed to stabilize wages and salaries within the general economic stabilization goals and coverage determination developed by the Council. Such procedures shall include, but not be limited to, those necessary to- (1) decide individual cases brought to its attention (including requests for exceptions); (2) recommend to the Department of Justice enforcement action designated to assure compliance; (3) maintain liaison to insure consistency between the Pay Board and the Price Commission and other organizational units of the economic stabilization program; and (4) maintain liaison with and augment the efforts of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service by providing such mediation efforts as might be necessary to obtain the voluntary compliance of parties to labor disputes with actions of the Board. 

2. There is hereby delegated to the Chairman of the Pay Board such authority vested in the Council by Section 4(a), 5, and 15 of the Executive Order as is necessary to perform the functions specified in section 1. 

3. All executive departments and agencies shall provide such necessary assistance to the Chairman as may be permitted by law. 

4. The Chairman may redelegate to any agency, instrumentality, or official of the United States any authority under this Executive order, and may, in carrying out the functions delegated to it by this Executive order, utilize the services of any other agencies, Federal or State, as may be available and appropriate. 

5. This order shall be effective upon the appointment and entry on duty of the Chairman of the Pay Board.

Delegation of Authority from CLC to the Treasury Department 

¶ 8403 

Cost of Living Council Order No. 5: Delegation of Authority Concerning Implementation of Stabilization of Prices, Rents, Wages, and Salaries, Novem ber 12, 1971: 

Pursuant to the Economic Stabilization Act of 1970 as amended (hereinafter referred to as the Act), and the authority delegated to the Cost of Living Council by Executive Order No. 11627 (hereinafter referred to as the 

Executive order) it is hereby ordered as follows: 

1. There is hereby delegated to the Secretary of the Treasury (hereinafter referred to as the Secretary), subject to the general policy guidance of ¶ 8403

and coordination with the Cost of Living Council (hereinafter referred to as the Council) and in accordance with the general policy of the Act, authority to interpret, implement, administer, monitor, and enforce the stabilization of prices, rents, wages, and salaries pursuant to the coverage, classifications, and implementation procedures established by the Council. Such functions will include, but not be limited to, the following: (a) Operation and maintenance of local service and compliance centers established in support of the economic stabilization program in Standard Metropolitan Statistical Areas and such other places as the Secretary may determine; (b) Dissemination of information and guidance to the public; (c) Issuance of rulings and the receiving, analyzing, and responding to inquiries relating to the application of regulations and other guidance issued by the Council and the establishment and operation of an appeal procedure; (d) Receiving, analyzing, investigating, and preparing and forwarding recommendations upon applications for exceptions and exemptions from coverage, classifications, and the implementation procedures to the Council for decision; (e) Conducting monitoring investigations as to the effectiveness of the stabilization program; (f) Receiving, investigating, and resolving by obtaining compliance, where possible, complaints received with respect to program violations and recommending enforcement action to the Council, where necessary; (g) Making factual determinations on behalf of the Council in furtherance of any functions herein delegated; and (h) Maintaining adequate records and the making of periodic reports to the Council. 

2. All executive departments and agencies shall furnish such necessary. assistance to the Secretary as may be authorized by law. 

3. The Secretary may redelegate to any agency, instrumentality, or official of the United States any authority under this order, and may, in carrying out the functions delegated by this order, utilize the services of any other agencies, Federal or State, as may be available and appropriate. 

4. The Director, Office of Emergency Preparedness, shall continue to exercise responsibility and authority under Council Order No. 1 as necessary to complete actions in process and to effectuate an orderly transfer of functions to the Pay Board established by section 7 of the Executive order and the Price Commission established by section 8 of the Executive order. 

5. Nothing in this order shall be construed to limit or otherwise supersede the authority heretofore delegated to the Pay Board by Council Order 

No. 3 or to the Price Commission by Council Order No. 4. 

6. This order shall be effective at 12:01 a. m., November 14, 1971. 

By direction of the Council.
