Pay Board Statement 

¶ 8405 

Remarks of Chairman Boldt at Press Conference November 8, 1971: 

It is a pleasure to announce that the Pay Board has reached major policy decisions regarding the post-freeze period of the Economic Stabilization Program. 

It is fair to state that each and every member of the Board has worked on our problems with great dedication and diligence. For the past two weeks we have been working many hours every day to achieve a result as fair to all Americans, whatever their economic situation, as the complexities of the problems involved will permit. Issues are involved which allow for wide ranges of judgment and opinion, and some of them arouse strong feelings. 

I would be less than candid not to admit that viewpoints have been exchanged with considerable emphasis from time to time. 

However, I am confident that every member of the Board has done his utmost to reach satisfactory solutions to the initial issues resolved by the policies adopted tonight.

Briefly stated, the substance of the policies adopted are: 

1. When these policies become effective, new pay decisions will be subject to a general standard authorizing up to 52% increase per year. This standard will be subject to periodic review. 

2. Pay increases scheduled for some future date, under a contract already in effect, will be permitted, excepting those which are found to be unreasonably inconsistent with the Board's criteria. 

3. Retroactive increases for pay raises denied during the freeze will only be approved in a limited number of carefully defined circumstances. 

This is a brief summary of our policy decisions adopted today. 

I believe these first policy decisions can and will provide a starting point for a program which will achieve the ultimate goal of ending inflation. 

With the understanding, cooperation and support of the vast majority of Americans, the program will succeed. On behalf of my colleagues and myself, we ask the American people to give us that cooperation. 

We will now pass out a copy of the actual plan as adopted by the Board as well as a copy of these remarks. 

The public members of the Board are here with me and we will be able to take just a few of your questions. ¶ 8406 

Statement of the Business Members of the Pay Board: 

The Business Members of the Pay Board endorse the pay standards adopted by the Board today as an effective and equitable part of the overall national program to limit the rise of inflation to no more than 2-3% by the end of 1972, to encourage substantial growth in business activity, to reduce unemployment, and to bolster the American position in foreign trade. 

Reaching these pay standards was not easy. The Business Members viewed the process not as just another collective bargaining negotiation, but rather as an effort of 15 responsible citizens to reach the goals set forth by the President. ¶ 8405

We felt that all of America needed an immediate and understandable statement of the general controls to be effective in Phase II. We have concurred in the program adopted. We regret that the Labor Members did not make the vote unanimous, but we hope that, as Americans united to achieve the national objective, there will be broad cooperation in that program. 

The Pay Board program is simple and understandable, with a single pay standard of 5.5% annually. It is equitable and fair to all, requiring almost every American to make some sacrifice, as any control program must do. 

It is timely, giving the business and labor communities an opportunity to plan in advance for Phase II activities. 

There is much unfinished work in administering the program. Its ultimate success will depend upon the voluntary cooperation of all Americans. 

As a special word to the business community, we do not minimize the difficulties or burdens which will face business in the months ahead. We urge the most complete understanding and cooperation. We are confident that our goals can be met within the year, and that all Americans will be benefitted by the effort. 

Robert C. Bassett 

Benjamin F. Biaggini 

Virgil B. Day

L. F. McCollum 

Rocco C. Siciliano

Rumsfeld Statement on Phase Two Reporting Classifications and Exemptions (November 10, 1971) 

¶ 8407 After consultation with the Pay Board and the Price Commission, the Cost of Living Council has reached a series of decisions to implement Phase 

II of the President's Economic Stabilization Program. 

These decisions apply to price and pay adjustments, and are designed to provide equity as well as an approach to monitor and restrain price and pay increases during the post freeze period, which begins on November 14. 

The procedures we have devised provide a flexible and suitable framework for arriving at equitable solutions to the complex issues of pay and prices. 

It is important to note that the procedures are designed to work in a way that reduces red tape to a minimum and does not require great numbers of people for administration. 

The Cost of Living Council has increased the number of exempt areas, those not covered by controls.

I will not go into detail on the procedural decisions or the coverage policy, but I would like to briefly outline those areas. After that, I will take questions relating to the two papers that have been distributed. 

The pay and price classifications are set out in three tiers-prenotification, reporting, and "other procedures." All three of these categories are subject to the standards and criteria developed by the Pay Board and the Price Commission. 

Price Classifications

Reporting procedures for price adjustments vary depending on the amount of annual sales or revenues reported by a firm in its most recent fiscal year. 

¶ 8407

(1) Firms with sales of $100 million or more must prenotify the Price Commission on proposed price adjustments and obtain approval. (2) Those with sales of between $50 million and $100 million must make quarterly reports to the Price Commission on changes in prices, costs and profits. (3) All other firms are not required to prenotify or report on a regular basis, but will be subject to the standards and criteria that the Price Commission will establish. 

Pay Classifications

Reporting procedures on pay adjustments are based on the number of employees affected. (1) When 5,000 or more employees are affected, prenotification of pay adjustments and approval by the Pay Board is required. (2) When between 1,000 and 5,000 employees are affected, information must be furnished as to the amount of the pay adjustment and the number of employees affected. This must be done at the time the adjustment becomes effective. (3) Generally, when fewer than 1,000 employees are involved, monitoring and spot checks will be used to assure compliance. 

Procedures are being adopted by the Pay Board and Price Commission to insure that, when appropriate, a firm's price adjustments will receive the same degree of scrutiny as its pay adjustments. Exemptions Since the freeze was put into effect on August 15, certain exemptions from the freeze have been permitted. These exemptions were permitted for a variety of reasons, consistent with the President's desire to impose only those controls necessary to turn back the tide of inflation and achieve reasonable price stability. During the post-freeze period, some new items and categories have been exempted. In every case the decision has been made in the light of the President's policy of removing controls as quickly as conditions warrant. 

Some examples of new and continued exemptions are: 

Raw agricultural products;

Art objects, antiques and handicraft objects; 

State and local taxes and fines; 

Exports and international shipping rates;

The initial transaction on imported products; Financial securities; 

Dues to non-profit organizations.

CLC Coordination To assure consistency in matters of policy and operations, the Pay Board and Price Commission and the Cost of Living Council are developing liaison procedures. These will include an exchange of appropriate information concerning pay and price adjustments and will enable the Cost of Living Council to monitor the overall operation of the Economic Stabilization Program and to coordinate actions of the three bodies on a National level and in the field.

Additional Press Conferences 

¶ 8408 

November 10, 1971, press conference of Donald Rumsfeld, Director of Cost of Living Council, Dr. Marvin Kosters, Associate Director for Policy and Plan ning of the CLC, and J. Maloney, General Counsel of the CLC:

MR. GREENER: Ladies and gentlemen: 

The press briefing today is on Coverage and Classification. As most of you know, the briefing will be by Mr. Donald Rumsfeld, Counsel to the President, and Director of the Cost of Living Council. I will ask all of you to stay until the end of the briefing. 

There will be a brief opening statement, and then we will be open for questions. 

MR. RUMSFELD: Thank you, Bill. 

To assist in the briefing I have Mr.

Joe Maloney, the General Counsel of the Cost of Living Council, and Dr. Marvin Kosters, the Associate Director for Policy and Planning.

After consultation with the Pay Board and the Price Commission, the Cost of Living Council has reached a series of decisions to implement Phase II 

of the President's Economic Stabilization Program, These decisions apply to price and pay adjustments, and are designed to provide equity as well as an approach to monitor and restrain price and pay increases during the post freeze period, which begins on November 14.

The procedures we have devised provide a flexible and suitable framework for arriving at equitable solutions to the complex issues of pay and prices. It is important to note that the procedures are designed to work in a way that reduces red tape to a minimum and does not require great numbers of people for administration.

The Cost of Living Council has increased the number of exempt areasthat is to say, those areas not covered by controls-from what existed during the freeze period.

I will not go into detail on the procedural decisions, or the coverage policy, but I would like to briefly outline those areas. After that, I will take questions relating to the papers that have been distributed. 

You see the chart on the right: The Pay and Price classifications are set out in three tiers: Pre-notification; Reporting; and Non-reporting. 

All three of those categories are subject to the standards and criteria developed by the Pay Board and the Price Commission. 

Reporting procedures for price adjustments vary, depending on the amount of annual sales, or revenues, reported by a firm in its most recent fiscal year.

As you see, firms with sales of $100 million, or over, must pre-notify the Price Commission on proposed price adjustments, and obtain approval. 

Those with sales of between $50 million and $100 million, must make quarterly reports to the Price Commission on changes in prices, costs and profits. ¶ 8408

All other firms are not required to pre-notify or report on a regular basis, but will be subject to the standards and criteria that the Price Commission will establish.

Reporting procedures on the pay adjustments are based on the number of employees affected.

When 5,000 or more employees are affected, pre-notification of pay adjustments and approval by the Pay Board is required. 

When between 1,000 and 5,000 employees are affected, information must be furnished as to the amount of the pay adjustment, and the number of employees affected. This must be done at the time the adjustment becomes effective. 

Generally, when fewer than 1,000 employees are involved, monitoring and spot checks will be used to assure compliance.

Procedures have been adopted by the Pay Board and the Price Commission to insure that, when appropriate, a firm's price adjustments will receive the same degree of scrutiny as its pay adjustments. 

Now, as to coverage: You have a separate piece of paper on that. 

Since the freeze was put into effect on August 15, certain exemptions from the freeze have been permitted. These exemptions were permitted for a variety of reasons, consistent with the President's desire to impose only those controls necessary to turn back the tide of inflation, and achieve reasonable price stability. During the post-freeze period, some new items and categories have been exempted. In every case, the decision has been made in the light of the President's policy of removing controls as quickly as conditions warrant. 

You have a listing of those specific items.

To assure consistency in matters of policy and operations between the elements of the Economic Stabilization Program, and the Pay Board, the Price Commission, and the Cost of Living Council, we are developing liaison procedures with those groups. This will include an exchange of appropriate information concerning pay and price adjustments and will enable the Cost of Living Council to monitor the overall operation of the Economic Stabilization Program, and to coordinate the actions of the three bodies at the National level, and in the field. 

One additional point: 

On August 15, the President announced the freeze for 90 days.

On October 7, he announced the outline of the Phase II, or post-freeze, Economic Stabilization Program. 

Since October 7, the Pay Board, the Price Commission, the Cost of Living Council, and others, have been working to put it in place. 

As of midnight, November 13, assuming the regulations are properly printed in the Federal Register, as we anticipate they will be, the freeze will have been modified. We will have moved from Phase I to the post-freeze period, by modifying the freeze and, in effect, making the transition to controls. 

The change will be as follows: (1) There will be changes in coverage. 

You have the paper that indicates that. (2) There will be announcements with respect to classification and reporting procedures. 

¶ 8408

(3) The Pay Board has announced its standards and criteria, and will have issued regulations. (4) The Price Commission will have issued their standards and criteria, and regulations will have been issued. 

I think the important point, here, is that the freeze does not become a total thaw, as of midnight, November 13, but rather, we move and make that transition from a freeze to controls.

The goal, obviously, is to achieve reasonable price stability, and the changes that have been announced, and will be announced during the remainder of the week, are aimed toward that end. 

There will be a lot of questions. You don't engage, in my judgment, in something as complex as we are now embarked on without having a great many questions from people all across the Country who have decisions to make and who, personally, have concern, and a need to know that information promptly and in a responsive way.

I guess I would end my comments by thanking those of you here and, in fact, the Communications Media generally, for the splendid help during the freeze period. It is a complicated business. I would hope, as we go through the coming weeks-where there will be a great many questions-that we will have your continued cooperation and assistance. I think it is important for all of the people of the Country, as well as the economy, generally. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Rumsfeld, where do Government employees, specifically teachers-local employees; State employees; and Federal employees come under the three tier system for pay increases? 

MR. RUMSFELD: The State and Local Government Advisory Committee is being announced, I believe, this afternoon, by the White House-the members. The Pay Board will be addressing the question, as to how they will handle State and local Governmental employees, later this week. There will be, possibly-we presently have some information before the Pay Board and the Price Commission as to Federal employees, for their comment and advice, and there may be an announcement with respect to Federal employees later in the week.

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Why were public utilities not included in the exemptions in the freeze?

MR. RUMSFELD: Again, the Cost of Living Council addressed the question of public utilities, and consulted with the Pay Board and the Price Commission. The decision was made not to exempt public utilities in the way that the areas being released today are exempted. 

How they will be specifically handled, will be something that will be announced, presumably, by the Pay Board and the Price Commission. 

MEMBER OF THE PRESS: Mr. Rumsfeld, there are a lot of large companies that negotiate on a local basis, and they may have many more than 5,000 employees, but the bargaining units are broken up into smaller numbers. 

What will their situation be? 

MR. RUMSFELD: Well, I believe in your paper there is an explanation.

It is at the middle portion of page 2 of the paper titled: Price and Pay 

Classification. 

¶ 8408

It says that a pay adjustment is a decision involving a general increase in salaries, wages, and fringe benefits, either through a collective bargaining process, or through actions by an employer, or group of employers.

Price Commission Statement 

¶ 8409 

Remarks by Price Commission Chairman C. Jackson Grayson at Press Con ference November 11, 1971.

I would like to introduce to you the Members of the Price Commission. 

To my left, John Queenan; J. Wilson Newman; Dr. Marina Whitman; Bill 

Coleman, and Bob Lanzillotti.

One of the Members, who is absent-Governor Scranton-planned to be here, but he had an engagement and asked me to say his proxy rests with me, and he supports our statement unanimously.

This morning, the Price Commission adopted the basic guidelines for achieving the President's Stabilization Program under Phase II. We are determined and I speak for every member of this Commission-to reduce the rate of inflation by providing price guidelines and standards to cover sectors of the economy.

Our principal objective is to bring down the rate of inflation from 2 to 3% by the end of 1972. This has been the policy enunciated by the Cost of 

Living Council and is, also, the goal of the Price Commission. 

These guidelines, which have just been distributed to you, give the general framework. Specific regulations are now being drafted, and will be available by the termination of Phase I at the end of the freeze. 

There will be controls and guidelines which will continue into Phase II, and these are contained in the regulations. 

The policies of this Price Commission are designed, and we are determined, to achieve a goal of holding the average price increase across the economy to no more than 2% per year.

Now, I would like to make some very general remarks that highlight things in this statement.

I said that we would try and hold the standards and guidelines for average price increases to no more than 22%. Now, this does not meanand I want to emphasize this-that every price increase in the economy must be exactly 22%, or no more than 22%. This means that some prices will go down. This means that some prices will increase more than 2%. 

So people should not expect, in this country, that every price increase is limited, by any firm, to exactly 2%.

We are determined that, in the aggregate, across the entire economy, the rate of price level changes will be no more than 22%.

The basic policy is that prices will not increase except where justified by costs incurred on or after November 14, and where we take into account productivity gains. This basic policy is one which we have adopted; also, it is that prices will not be increased to recover, retroactively, costs that may have been incurred in the period from August 14 to November 14.

The criteria we have for the success of this program depends heavily on voluntary compliance. Without the support of the people of this nation to go along with the President's program and help hold down the rate of inflation, I assure you that the mechanisms we have designed will not work. 

Everyone in this country has to realize that we must hold down inflation. 

Our price guidelines are designed to do this; to preserve fairness and, also, price firmness. ¶ 8409 

1972, Commerce Clearing House, Inc

Not everyone will like the standards and guidelines that have been promulgated, but we have done the best that we can as an entire Commission to be sure that we are achieving the objectives, and to be as fair as possible. 

I think you will see that we have not created an elaborate set of control mechanisms. We are determined that these standards and guidelines will accomplish the objectives, but we are not here to set up a bureaucracy to enforce a very large control mechanism for the economy. 

Our desire is to achieve the goals, but we would like to de-emphasize the control mechanisms as rapidly as possible, consistent with the overall goals. 

Now, we are going to continually review the implementation, the pattern of implementation, of these standards and guidelines across the country. 

There will be monitoring, and we will make revisions in our standards, as appropriate, in order to be sure that we reach our goal. 

I want to express appreciation to many people who have helped us in getting these standards and guidelines formulated. I asked for people across the Nation to send in letters to me, with ideas, and we have had, at least, more than 5,000 responses, and they are still coming in. Not only do you see, in these letters, ideas, but also the emotionality of the average person concerned with what is happening as a result of inflation. 

We have also held informal conversations to receive inputs from people from labor; from Government; from business; from consumers; and each member of the Commission has also held conferences with any number of people. 

We have been anxious to receive as many inputs as possible. We want the public; we want the Nation, to be informed because, as I said, without voluntary support, this system will not work. So it is our intention to make available the information that we are collecting about the economy and how we are doing, relative to our overall goals. 

I have asked Bill Helmantoler-who is our Director of Public Affairsto insure that the word is put out to the nation about what is happening in this program. 

I ask each of you gentlemen of the Press to contact him whenever you want information about our activities, so that you can keep in touch, also. For myself, for my own personal style, I would like every press conference to be on the record. I want to be very frank about what is happening, and I want to assure you that these general statements as opening remarks represent a unanimous position on the part of the entire Price Commission, and I want to also express my appreciation to all the members, for the dedication that they exhibited in joining this Commission, and for the time and effort that they have devoted to reaching the position this morning. 

Thank you.

Rumsfeld Press Conference of November 19, 1971 

¶ 8410 

November 19, 1971 Press Conference of Donald Rumsfeld, Counsellor to the President and Director of the Cost of Living Council: 

MR. WARREN: You have two releases this afternoon. The President is appointing the chairmen and members of the Committee on the Health 

Services Industry and the Committee on State and Local Government Cooperation. 

¶ 8410

Don Rumsfeld, Counsellor to the President and Director of the Cost of 

Living Council, is here this afternoon. We thought it might be helpful for him to run through this with you and take your questions. Don? 

MR. RUMSFELD: Thank you, Jerry.

I will just make two or three points. The chairmen and the members of the two advisory committees, one on State and Local Government Cooperation and the other on the Health Services Industry, are listed on the paper. 

I would underline the fact that both of these groups are advisory, and they would not infringe on the grant of power made through the Executive Order and the Delegation agreements to the Pay Board and the Price Commission. 

However, as the President indicated in his speech on October 7th, it was felt that these areas had a substantial impact on the economy and on inflation, and that the Cost of Living Council, the Pay Board and the Price Commission, all of whom will be receiving the advice of these two groups, could benefit by having a committee in each of these areas which had on it people who were involved in those particular problems, were knowledgeable about them, and were interested in seeing that they were handled in a way that was sensible from the standpoint of those two particular areas. 

I would like to take just a minute and make one other comment before responding to questions on these subjects. 

This afternoon at 2:00 o'clock we had a press conference at the Cost of 

Living Council which involved the announcement of coverage questions; that is to say, areas of the economy that would be exempt from controls during the Phase 2 period, and also announced the classification or three-tier criteria that the President indicated in his speech would be forthcoming. 

So, where we have been and where we are and where we are going is essentially this: On August 15th the President announced the freeze. On 

October 7th he announced the structure of Phase 2. On October 15th the 

Executive Order and Delegation agreements were signed and sent forward. 

On October 19th the legislation was sent to the Congress. On October 22nd the members of the Pay Board and Price Commission were appointed and began their work. On November 8th the Pay Board announced its standards and criteria. On November 10th, today, we released the coverage and classi fication and the State and Local Government Cooperation and Health Services Industry Committees. 

It is anticipated that tomorrow the Price Commission will complete their work on standards and criteria and make their announcements. On November 

12th, Friday, it is anticipated that the transfer of responsibility from the Office of Emergency Preparedness to the Internal Revenue Service, as far as service and compliance with the economic stabilization program, will take place. 

It is also anticipated that the specific regulations which are required to be printed in the Federal Register will be completed Friday morning, regulations that involve the four major areas I described: pay standards and criteria, price standards and criteria, coverage, and the classification questions. 

It is anticipated that the State and Local Government Cooperation Committee and the Health Services Industry Committee will be meeting early next week, so we will know what is going to happen at midnight the night of the 

13th, when the President indicated the freeze would end.

I would like to emphasize one final point: The freeze at that moment will be modified and will no longer exist as a freeze, but, in fact, there will be controls. The controls will affect every portion of the economy except ¶ 8410

those that have been specifically exempted. The actual transition, then, from 

Phase 1, a freeze, to controls, which represent the economic stabilization program, will have been accomplished. 

It seems to me there is one last point that I would like to mention, and that is that what we are doing here is dealing with the economy of the United States, something that is exceedingly complex, something that involves millions and millions of decisions, and there are inevitably going to be a great many questions. Each new announcement, of necessity, opens up a new level beneath it of questions. 

The answers to those questions are exceedingly important to the American people. They involve their lives, their pay, their prices, and each is important. 

I, personally, would want to say that I think the communications media has been exceedingly helpful during the freeze period in communicating the information throughout the country, and I, for one, am grateful and appreciative, and recognize it, and I know the people who have been involved in the Phase 1 activity also share that sentiment. Questions?

Q. Don, has there been any communication at all from the Cost of 

Living Council or you to the Pay Board in terms of what apparently is now a willingness to reconsider the 10-to-5 hardline vote on retroactive pay increases? 

There has been an indication that there may be a softening of that decision now, subject to reconsideration. 

MR. RUMSFELD: There have not been communications of any nature by me with respect to that vote. I am in constant touch, as is my staff on the 

Cost of Living Council, with the staff on the Pay Board and Price Commission with respect to my responsibilities for coordination and in seeing that what takes place within the Board and Commission can, in fact, be implemented out in the field. 

But as far as the specific question you are asking, I would not even want to answer it in a way that would agree with what you are saying, because I think that the Delegation Agreements and the President's memorandum which he initialed have left the Pay Board and Price Commission a whole set of decisions which they are wrestling with and making judgments on. 

I think tomorrow the Pay Board meets, tomorrow afternoon, and they will be addressing questions involving the level of decision below the announcement they made on Monday; that is to say, they will be reviewing, as I understand it, and I do not want to be in a position to speak for them, but it is my understanding that they will be addressing the regulations and addressing questions that are a level below the basic one decided. 

Q. Is it your impression that there may be a softening of the line against retroactive pay increases for those negotiated contracts? 

MR. RUMSFELD: You would have to discuss that with the members of the Pay Board, unless you mean a softening of the line by the White House. 

The White House has taken no position on retroactive increases, so there is nothing to soften or harden, if you are talking about the White House or me or the Cost of Living Council. That has not been addressed. 

Q. I mean within the Pay Board.

MR. RUMSFELD: I would not want to characterize it. 

Q. When are these committees appointed today going to meet for the first time?

Monday; but I think early in the week for sure. I understand one of the members' wives just had a baby. That might delay it one day.

MR. RUMSFELD: That would be something we would work out with them as they gather and assemble and develop an agenda. 

Q. Mr. Rumsfeld, does the Pay Board's decision on the allowable level of increases, the 5½ percent, apply to State and municipal employees, and does it apply to the military pay increase granted by Congress? 

MR. RUMSFELD: Today we announced a whole series of exemptions; that is, areas that will not be affected by the controls. Neither of the ones you mentioned were included; therefore, the presumption at this moment should be that unless something is specifically exempted from controls, it will, in fact, be covered.

Now, with respect to Federal employees, obviously there is a need for somewhat separate handling for a variety of reasons which I do not care to go into at the moment. The Cost of Living Council has been discussing that. 

Under our arrangement, we are consulting with the Pay Board and Price Commission on that subject, and it is conceivable that later in the week there might be an announcement with respect to that. 

As to State and local government, I cannot say how the Pay Board will deal with that specific area. I think in part it will be a result of the advice and counsel they receive from this Advisory Committee. So I guess that answers both pieces.

Q. Were there any health industry exemptions on that list?

Q. Phase 2 becomes official on Sunday?

MR. RUMSFELD: It should. The freeze is on until it is modified legally and by competent authority; that is, by the Cost of Living Council, the Pay Board and the Price Commission. So our present plan is that the regulations will be available for printing in the Federal Register at the deadline date, which I understand is 11:00 o'clock on Friday. If they fail to arrive there for some reason-for example, if the Pay Board did not finish its work on the regulations tomorrow-it is conceivable that the freeze would be extended for a day or two until they could comply with the legal requirement that they be printed in the Federal Register. 

So the freeze continues until it is modified. We anticipate that it will be modified and it will be modified in some ways, anyway. For example, the exemption I announced today will clearly go into effect, because we control the regulation there, and it will be accomplished by that time.

In the simplest sense, without prejudging how they will decide to handle prices tomorrow, I think what you should look for is the announcement of their decision as made, the release of the regulations, the communication out across the country of the specific regulations with respect to the four areas: pay, price, coverage and classification. Then everyone will look at that and there will be a whole set of questions they will have. 

A large group will immediately say, "Well, I fit in Tier 1," or "I am exempt," or "My pay or price situation is reasonably answered by what they have said." Others will look at it and say, "I am kind of on the borderline,"

¶ 8410

¶ 8411 

Phase Rulings in Effect Until Modified 

The Cost of Living Council has announced that the regulations which made the 90-day program a "freeze" will be modified to make the system more effective. Donald Rumsfeld, Director of the Council, stated that there will be no automatic ending on November 13 of present freeze rules on wages, prices, and rents. They will be changed only by the introduction of new regulations, thus preventing a gap that would occur if present rules were allowed to end before new ones had been instituted.

Rumsfeld noted that, as stated in the President's Executive Order of October 15, the provisions of the economic stabilization program which have been in force since August 15 will continue until they are specifically modified by the Pay Board, Price Commission, or the Cost of Living Council. However, changes will occur only through explicit action taken by competent authority. 

It is anticipated that initial modifications to the freeze rules will be announced prior to November 13. ¶ 8412 

President Welcomes Labor's Participation on Pay Board 

On the heels of organized labor's announcement of their willingness to participate on the Pay Board 

President Nixon issued the following statement:

I welcome the participation of organized labor in the work of the Pay Board and in helping make the Nation's efforts at price and wage stabilization succeed. Bringing the cost of living under control requires the public-spirited cooperation of all Americans, and in giving such cooperation, the leaders of organized labor have acted in the best interest of their own Members and of the Nation.

I also reaffirm my concern that the economy expand and attain full employment. Prompt action in the Senate on my tax proposals, which will create over ½ million jobs, is essential to attainment of this objective.

Proclamation No. 4074 Imposition of Supplemental Duty for Balance of Payments Purposes 

¶ 3012 WHEREAS, there has been a prolonged decline in the international monetary reserves of the United States, and our trade and international competitive position is seriously threatened and, as a result, our continued ability to assure our security could be impaired; 

WHEREAS, the balance of payments position of the United States requires the imposition of a surcharge on dutiable imports; 

WHEREAS, pursuant to the authority vested in him by the Constitution and the statutes, including, but not limited to, the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (hereinafter referred to as "the Tariff Act”), and the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 (hereinafter referred to as "the TEA"), the President entered into, and proclaimed tariff rates under, trade agreements with foreign countries; 

WHEREAS, under the Tariff Act, the TEA, and other provisions of law, the President may, at any time, modify or terminate, in whole or in part, any proclamation made under his authority; 

NOW, THEREFORE, I, RICHARD NIXON, President of the 

United States of America, acting under the authority vested in me by the Constitution and the statutes, including, but not limited to, the Tariff Act, and the TEA, respectively, do proclaim as follows: 

A. I hereby declare a national emergency during which I call upon the public and private sector to make the efforts necessary to strengthen the international economic position of the United States. 

B. (1) I hereby terminate in part for such period as may be necessary and modify prior Presidential Proclamations which carry out trade agreements insofar as such proclamations are inconsistent with, or proclaim duties different from, those made effective pursuant to the terms of this Proclamation. (2) Such proclamations are suspended only insofar as is required to assess a surcharge in the form of a supplemental duty amounting to 10 percent ad valorem. Such supplemental duty shall be imposed on all dutiable articles imported into the customs territory of the United States from outside thereof, which are entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption after 12:01 a. m., August 16, 1971, provided, however, that if the imposition of an additional duty of 10 per- 

Stabilization Program Guidelines

2 rate shall apply.

C. To implement section B of this Proclamation, the following new subpart shall be inserted after subpart B of part 2 of the Appendix to the Tariff Schedules of the United States: 

SUBPART C-TEMPORARY MODIFICATIONS For Balance of PAYMENTS PURPOSES Subpart C headnotes: 

1. This subpart contains modifications of the provisions of the tariff schedules proclaimed by the President in Proclamation 4074. 

2. Additional duties imposed-The duties provided for in this subpart are cumulative duties which apply in addition to the duties otherwise imposed on the articles involved. The provisions for these duties are effective with respect to articles entered on and after 12:01 a. m., August 16, 1971, and shall continue in effect until modified or terminated by the President or by the Secretary of the Treasury (hereinafter referred to as the Secretary) in accordance with headnote 4 of this subpart. 

3. Limitation on additional duties-The additional 10 percent rate of duty specified in rate of duty column numbered 1 of item 948.00 shall in no event exceed that rate which, when added to the column numbered 1 rate imposed on the imported article under the appropriate item in schedules 1 through 7 of these schedules, would result in an aggregated rate in excess of the rate provided for such article in rate of duty column numbered 2. 

4. For the purposes of this subpart— (a) Delegation of authority to Secretary-The Secretary may from time to time take action to reduce, eliminate or reimpose the rate of additional duty herein or to establish exemption therefrom, either generally or with respect to an article which he may specify either generally or as the product of a particular country, if he determines that such action is consistent with safeguarding the balance of payments position of the United States. (b) Publication of Secretary's actions-All actions taken by the Secretary hereunder shall be in the form of modifications of this subpart published in the FEDERAL REGISTER. Any action reimposing the additional duties on an article exempted therefrom by the Secretary shall be effective only with respect to articles entered on and after the date of publication of the action in the FEDERAL REGISTER. (c) Authority to prescribe rules and regulations-The Secretary is authorized to prescribe such rules and regulations as he determines to be necessary or appropriate to carry out the provisions of this subpart. ¶ 3012

Inventory Control 

Q: Many businesses have a serious inventory problem due to the import surcharge. How can such businesses pass on the surcharge when they have thousands of different items in inventory, with many new shipments arriving daily, and they can pass on the surcharge on some items and not on others?

A: Where possible, surcharge and non-surcharge items should be stored separately. Where this cannot be done, the wholesaler may elect to charge the base period ceiling price for each item that was in effect prior to August 15, 1971, until a quantity has been sold for each item equal to the quantity on hand prior to the arrival of items with a surcharge added. He may then charge at the old rate plus the exact surcharge.

Import Surcharge 13050 Shipment Date 

¶ 3050.05 

Date of exportation.—Q: If a ship calls at several ports in a foreign country and leaves that country directly for the United States, what is the date of exportation?

A: The date the ship leaves each port will be the date of exportation for goods laden at that port. 

Q: What is the date of exportation when the ship does not leave that country directly for the United States? For instance, take a case in which a ship calls at several ports in country A, proceeds to a port in country B and loads, then returns to a port of country A before leaving for the United States.

A: For all merchandise laden in country A, the date of exportation is the date the ship last leaves the jurisdiction of country A. For merchandise laden in country B, the date of exportation is the date the ship leaves the jurisdiction of country B. 

Q: What about goods shipped by rail or truck from Canada and Mexico?

A: The date of exportation is the date the carrier crosses the border into the United States. 

Q: I ordered merchandise from Austria. It crossed the border into Germany on August 14, but was not shipped from Germany until 

August 20. What is the date of exportation?

A: August 14. The date the merchandise leaves the jurisdiction of the country of exportation is the date of exportation. 

Q: Is the date of exportation determined in terms of the local time of the exporting country?

A: No. In order not to be subject to the additional duty under this exemption, an article must have been exported before the equivalent local time of 12:01 a. m., Eastern Daylight Time, August 16, 1971. 

.01 Treasury Dept. Q&A #2, Sep tember 15, 1971. ¶ 3050.10

Goods on high seas.—Q: I had several shipments which were on the high seas destined for the United States before August 16. Will I have to pay the 10 percent additional duty?

A: No.

Long-term contracts.-Q: Does the additional duty apply to merchandise purchased under a long-term, irrevocable contract?

No. 3 (3-1-72) ¶3050.25 

Refund of erroneous collection.—Q: I have paid 10 percent additional duty on merchandise which was exported to the United States before August 16, 1971, and which is not now subject to the additional duty. Will my money be refunded? 

A: Yes. If there has been an erroneous collection of ad valorem additional duty, the entry will be liquidated as soon as possible, and a refund will be processed. If immediate liquidation is not possible, and a refund is requested for the erroneous additional duty, appropriate action will be taken to authorize the refund without awaiting liquidation (.01). 

Q: Does this apply to a warehouse withdrawal? 

A: Yes. However, insofar as possible, the refund of the erroneous additional duty in such a case will be made by adjustment on subsequent withdrawals (.01).

Q: Will the import surcharge have to be refunded to customers at all levels of distribution?

A: No, the lifting of the import surcharge imposes no requirement that refunds be made. The surcharge paid on inventoried items is an allowable cost and may be considered in pricing (.05).

Tariff-Rate Quota 

Q: What is the difference between an absolute quota and a tariffrate quota?

A: An absolute quota limits the total quantity which may be imported within a given period of time. A tariff-rate quota establishes a higher rate of duty once a given quantity has been imported. 

.01 Treasury Dept. Q&A #2, Sep tember 15, 1971.

¶ 3075 Cost of Living Council Order No. 2 

Pursuant to the authority vested in the Council by Executive Order No. 11615, it is hereby ordered that there are exempted from the prohibitions of section 1 of that order articles imported into the Customs territory of the United States from outside thereof, to the extent, but only to the extent, that any price higher than that permitted under that order is to offset the supplemental duty imposed by Proclamation No. 4074 and paid, directly or indirectly, by the person charging, assessing, or receiving, the higher price. Any increase in price, whether at wholesale or retail or otherwise, which is greater than that necessary to offset the supplemental duty actually passed on to, and paid by, the person charging, assessing, or receiving, the higher price, shall be deemed to be in violation of that order.

August 24, 1971 

Secretary of the Treasury John B. Connally announced certain exemptions from the 10 percent ad valorem duty imposed on all duti able imports under Presidential Proclamation 4074. The exemptions relate in general to quota restricted merchandise. Additional Duty 

Order No. 2 is effective as of 12:01 a. m., August 16, 1971. ¶ 3081

The exempted items cover: 

(1) Fresh, chilled, or frozen beef, veal, mutton, and goat meat, irrespective of country of origin, provided for in items 106.10 and 

106.20, Tariff Schedules of the United States (TSUS). (2) Articles subject to import restrictions proclaimed pursuant to Section 22 of the Agricultural Adjustment Act. These are set forth in Part 3 of the Appendix to the Tariff Schedules and include certain milks, creams, butter, butter substitutes, cheeses, cheese substitutes, malted milk, articles of milk and cream, chocolate, animal feeds containing milk or milk derivatives, ice cream, articles containing butterfat, wheat, peanuts, and cotton. (3) Crude oil, unfinished oils, finished oil products, and certain petrochemicals, which are described in Presidential Proclamation. 

3279, of March 10, 1959, as amended (24 F. R. 178). Shipments of these articles are normally covered by licenses issued by the office of the Oil Import Administration, Department of the Interior. This exemption also includes number 2 fuel oil of Canadian origin shipped overland from Canada into District I (which includes the New England states) and crude oil shipped by pipeline from Canada into District 5 (which includes Alaska, Arizona, California, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, and Washington). 475.05 475.10 475.15 475.25 475.30 475.35

There are 64 categories of these products. (5) Sugar which is subject to quantitative controls administered by the Department of Agriculture. This sugar is usually provided for in items 155.20 through 155.30, of the Tariff Schedules.

.01 Articles Exempt from Additional Schedules of the United States, August Duty Imposed under Subpart C of 31, 1971 (36 F. R. 17667, September Part 2 of the Appendix to the Tariff 3, 1971). 

Announcement of Treasury Department Additional Duty Order No. 3 

September 1, 1971 The Treasury Department announced today that it has exempted from the 10% additional import duty merchandise which had already been exported from foreign countries to the United States when the surcharge became effective on August 16.

The order exempts merchandise exported for the U. S. prior to 

August 16 which: -Is tied up by the dock strike at West Coast ports, -Was aboard ships on the high seas enroute to the U. S., and -Is in bonded warehouses or foreign trade zones within the U. S. 

However, the merchandise in warehouses and zones must be withdrawn by October 1, 1971, in order to qualify for the exemption. 

Eugene T. Rossides, Assistant Secretary of the Treasury for Enforcement, Tariff & Trade Affairs, and Operations, said that the order is based on the determination that the date of shipment is the preferable date to achieve consistency and equity and to prevent harsh retroactive effects of the application of the additional 10% import duty, while at the same time carrying out the President's purpose of safeguarding the balance of payments position of the United States. ¶ 3082 

Stabilization Program Guidelines

Import Surcharge 

3075 

Without the exemption announced today, importers would have been forced to pay the additional duty on merchandise already enroute to the United States and over which they had no control. This would have placed them at an unfair disadvantage compared to importers whose cargoes were already in the United States. Many small importers claimed they faced possible bankruptcy without the exemption. 

Assistant Secretary Rossides pointed out that this is a one-time, non-recurring exemption. It affects only merchandise which at the time of the Proclamation was already on its way to the United States, in the United States, or in its ports, and which would have entered the country in any event.

Although the order affects merchandise being brought in by air, truck or rail transport before August 16, the bulk of the goods involved were aboard ships when the additional duty was announced. 

The Treasury has no accurate calculation of the total value of dutiable merchandise involved, but it is estimated to be in excess of $1.5 billion.

The order, titled "Treasury Department Additional Duty Order 

No.

3" will be published in the Federal Register on Friday, September 3, 1971.
